lessons.title: Spotting problems in sows and boars
lessons.html:
Know what normal looks like

Walk through the piggery every day and look at every pig. A healthy sow or boar is alert, gets up to eat, eats well, walks easily, and has normal dung (not runny, not hard and dry). Its skin is clean and pink or its normal colour. It breathes quietly.

Abnormalities in sows

What you seeWhat it might mean
Not eating, lying down, hot to touchFever or infection
Hard, hot, red udder after farrowing; piglets hungry and squealingMastitis or no milk (agalactia)
Smelly discharge from the vulvaInfection of the womb
Sow strains for a long time during farrowing with no pigletDifficult birth: call the supervisor at once
Part of the womb or rectum pushed outProlapse: emergency
Sow does not come on heat after weaning, or returns to heat after matingFertility problem
Early birth of dead pigletsAbortion: may be a disease

Abnormalities in boars

  • Lame or swollen feet and legs: a lame boar cannot mount.
  • Not interested in sows (low libido).
  • Swollen testicles or sores on the sheath or penis.
  • Too fat or too thin.

Abnormalities in all adult pigs

  • Coughing and fast breathing.
  • Diarrhoea or blood in dung.
  • Skin problems: scratching, red patches, mange.
  • Fighting wounds and bitten tails or ears.

Report every abnormal pig to your supervisor straight away, with its ear tag or pen number. Do not treat pigs yourself unless you have been trained and told to; medicines must be used as the label or the vet says. Some pig diseases, such as African swine fever, are controlled diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 and must be reported. Sudden deaths must always be reported at once.

lessons.title: Spotting problems in piglets
lessons.html:
The first weeks are the most dangerous

Most piglet deaths happen in the first days of life. Check the farrowing house several times a day.

Healthy piglets

  • Strong, active, drinking from the sow often.
  • Round belly after feeding.
  • Sleep together in a warm group, under the heat lamp or in the creep area.

Abnormalities in piglets

What you seeWhat it might mean
Watery yellow or white dung, dirty tail, thin pigletDiarrhoea (scours)
Legs sliding out sideways, cannot standSplay leg
Pale skin, weak, breathing fastAnaemia (iron shortage) or disease
Lump in the groin or at the navelHernia
Swollen joints, lameJoint infection
Small, weak piglet pushed away from teatsRunt; may starve
Piglets piled together and shiveringToo cold
Piglets lying far from the lamp, pantingToo hot
Flat, dead piglet next to the sowCrushed by the sow

What you can do

  • Keep the creep area warm, dry and free of draughts.
  • Make sure every piglet drinks colostrum (first milk) soon after birth.
  • Keep the pen clean and dry.
  • Report sick piglets at once, with the sow's number.
  • Remove dead piglets, record them and report the cause if you know it.

Piglets are usually given iron and other treatments according to the farm's health programme. Follow the vet's programme and the product label.

lessons.title: Weighing pigs and keeping records
lessons.html:
Why we weigh pigs

  • To check that pigs are growing well.
  • To work out feed amounts and medicine doses.
  • To know when pigs are ready for market.
  • To pick pigs that are not growing well.

How to weigh pigs

Piglets

  1. Use a small hanging scale with a bucket or a sling, or a platform scale.
  2. Set the scale to zero with the empty bucket.
  3. Lift the piglet gently, supporting its body. Do not lift by one leg or the ears.
  4. Put it in the bucket, wait for the scale to settle, read the mass in kg.
  5. Return it to the sow quickly.

Weaners, growers and adults

  1. Use a walk-in pig scale (crate scale).
  2. Check that the scale reads zero when empty.
  3. Move the pig calmly into the crate with a pig board. Close both gates.
  4. Wait until the pig stands still and read the mass.
  5. Let it out calmly.

Recording and reporting

Write on the weighing sheet: date, pig's ear tag or pen number, age or group, and mass. Example: 12/03, pen 4, weaner, 7.5 kg. Report to your supervisor any pig that is much lighter than its pen mates, and any pig that lost mass.

lessons.title: Managing the boar
lessons.html:
The boar is half the herd

The boar mates many sows, so his health and fertility affect every litter. A good boar manager keeps the boar fit, healthy, calm and fertile.

Housing

  • A strong pen with a dry, non-slip floor so he does not hurt his feet and legs.
  • Shade and cool conditions: heat stress lowers fertility.
  • Clean water at all times.
  • Where possible, a pen near the sows so they can see and smell him.

Feeding

Feed the boar the ration and amount the farm's feeding plan gives. Keep him in good condition: not too fat and not too thin. A fat boar is lazy and may hurt sows.

Using the boar

  • Follow the farm's mating plan for how often each boar is used. Overuse lowers fertility.
  • Take the sow to the boar's pen, or bring the boar to a mating pen with a good floor.
  • Watch the mating and record: date, sow number and boar number.
  • Young boars must be trained gently with quiet sows.

Health checks

  • Check feet, legs, testicles and sheath.
  • Keep his health programme up to date as the vet advises.
  • Report if sows mated by him often return to heat.

Safety with boars

  • Boars are strong and can attack. Never turn your back on a boar.
  • Always carry a pig board and know your escape route.
  • Do not enter a boar's pen alone if the farm rule says two people.

Key points

  • Check every pig daily and report abnormal pigs with their tag or pen number.
  • Watch piglets for scours, cold, weakness and crushing.
  • Weigh pigs on a zeroed scale and record date, number and mass.
  • Keep boars cool, fit, healthy and used according to the mating plan.
  • Never turn your back on a boar; carry a pig board.
